question: Which antibiotics are safe to use in kidney transplant patients with impaired graft function (reduced eGFR) requiring dose adjustment?

must_have: Names specific commonly used antibiotics with their renal handling (e.g. ceftriaxone usually needs no renal dose adjustment; cefepime requires dose reduction at reduced CrCl with neurotoxicity risk if unadjusted; amoxicillin/amoxicillin-clavulanate need adjustment in severe impairment; TMP-SMX needs dose reduction and potassium monitoring)
Flags aminoglycosides (gentamicin/amikacin/tobramycin) as nephrotoxic and NOT a renal-safe default for a vulnerable graft even where resistance data favor their coverage
Surfaces the immunosuppressant interaction axis: macrolides such as clarithromycin/erythromycin raise tacrolimus/cyclosporine levels (CYP3A) requiring trough monitoring
Every drug-specific claim is supported by evidence about THAT drug or class — no citations from unrelated (non-antibiotic) drug labels presented as antibiotic evidence
nice_to_have: Distinguishes eGFR from CrCl thresholds used on labels
Notes vancomycin needs individualized dosing with level monitoring
Keeps resistance-pattern findings (e.g. graft pyelonephritis empiric coverage) clearly separate from safety/dosing guidance

answer:
## Bottom line
For kidney transplant recipients with reduced eGFR, the evidence retrieved supports **CrCL-based individualized dosing of teicoplanin** (a glycopeptide) as one option with defined pharmacokinetic rationale [1][2], and notes teicoplanin is preferred over vancomycin for gram-positive infections in this population due to fewer nephrotoxic effects [3]. Beyond teicoplanin, the findings only establish the general principle that renal dose adjustment is standard practice [8][9][10][11] and point to two other agents (cefixime, gabapentin — the latter not an antibiotic) with labeled renal-adjustment requirements [4][5], but do not provide transplant-specific dosing data for a broader antibiotic list.

## Efficacy
- [[F]]Creatinine clearance (CrCL) was the only covariate significantly affecting teicoplanin clearance in renal transplant patients[[/F]], and standard (non-adjusted) dosing regimens failed to meet treatment needs for all patients in dosing simulations, supporting CrCL-based individualized loading and maintenance dosing [1][12] (these two findings restate the same result).
- [[F]]Higher-than-standard teicoplanin doses are needed to promptly achieve adequate drug exposure[[/F]] in renal transplant patients [2].
- Comparative studies show **no significant difference in antimicrobial activity between teicoplanin and vancomycin** for gram-positive infections including MRSA [3].
- Cefixime carries a distinct labeled section for renal dose adjustment [4], but no efficacy or exposure figures for this adjustment are given in the findings.

## Safety & adverse effects
| Agent | Renal-impairment consideration | Reported adverse-effect profile |
|---|---|---|
| Teicoplanin | CrCL-based dose individualization recommended [1][12]; higher-than-standard doses needed [2] | [[F]]Fewer adverse effects, including nephrotoxicity and infusion reactions, compared with vancomycin[[/F]] [3] |
| Vancomycin | Recommended glycopeptide alongside teicoplanin [3] | More nephrotoxicity and infusion reactions reported versus teicoplanin [3] |
| Cefixime | Labeled "Dose Adjustment in Renal Impairment" section exists [4] | Not reported in findings |

General principle: drug effects are altered in renal impairment, particularly for renally cleared drugs, and doses should be adjusted to the predicted reduction in clearance [9][10]; in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury, especially those needing renal replacement therapy, careful antimicrobial management is essential to avoid inappropriate therapy [6][7].

## Population
The teicoplanin pharmacokinetic findings apply specifically to **[[K]]renal (kidney) transplant patients[[/K]]** [1][2][3][12] — the population directly matching the question. The general renal-dosing principles [8][9][10][11] apply broadly to patients with acute or chronic kidney disease, not specifically transplant recipients. The critically-ill/AKI/renal-replacement-therapy findings [6][7] describe a related but distinct population (critically ill patients with AKI, not necessarily transplant recipients). Cefixime [4] and gabapentin [5] renal-adjustment labeling findings do not specify transplant patients.

## Evidence quality
The teicoplanin findings derive from a **population pharmacokinetics and dosing-optimization study** in renal transplant patients, using covariate analysis and dosing simulations [1][2][3][12] — this is [[R]]observational/PK-modeling evidence identifying a covariate (CrCL) and simulating dosing scenarios, not a randomized efficacy trial, so it supports dose-optimization rationale rather than demonstrated clinical outcome improvement[[/R]]. The comparative nephrotoxicity claim for teicoplanin vs vancomycin cites prior comparative studies referenced within this source [3], not a standalone systematic review presented here. The general renal-dosing statements [8][9][10][11] and the cefixime/gabapentin labeling [4][5] are drawn from prescribing information (dailymed) and general reference sources (StatPearls, CKD dosing guidance) — labeling and reference-level evidence, not trial data specific to transplant patients.

## Not addressed
The findings do not cover a broad panel of antibiotics (e.g., beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones) with transplant-specific renal dose-adjustment data, nor do they report clinical outcomes (infection cure rates, graft survival, mortality) associated with any renal-adjusted antibiotic regimen in transplant patients — the teicoplanin data are pharmacokinetic/simulation-based, not outcome trial data.

claims.text: In renal transplant patients, creatinine clearance (CrCL) was the only covariate found to significantly affect teicoplanin clearance, and standard dosing regimens were unable to meet treatment needs for all patients, so CrCL-based individualized dosing regimens (both loading and maintenance dose) are recommended.
claims.quote: Creatinine clearance (CrCL) was the only covariate that significantly affected teicoplanin clearance. Dosing simulation results showed that standard dosing regimens were unable to meet the treatment needs of all patients, and CrCL-based individual dosing regimens are recommended for both loading dose and maintaining dose.
claims.title: Population pharmacokinetics and dosing optimization of teicoplanin in renal transplant patients - PMC

claims.text: Teicoplanin dosing in renal transplant patients requires higher-than-standard doses to promptly achieve adequate drug exposure, reflecting the need for careful dose adjustment based on renal function in this population.

claims.title: Population pharmacokinetics and dosing optimization of teicoplanin in renal transplant patients - PMC

claims.text: Vancomycin and teicoplanin are the glycopeptide antibiotics currently recommended for treating gram-positive infections, including MRSA, in renal transplant patients, and comparative studies show similar antimicrobial activity between the two, but teicoplanin has fewer adverse effects such as nephrotoxicity and infusion reactions.
claims.quote: Vancomycin and teicoplanin are the glycopeptides currently recommended for the treatment of these infections (3–5).
